name: Kira Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I study business management, so my week is lectures on marketing and operations, plus group presentations that I always end up organising. I live at home with my parents, who run a small dry-cleaning shop, and I take the bus in. Weekends I work at a bakery from six in the morning, shaping rolls and serving the early queue.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's it like having parents who run a shop while you study business?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Strange but useful. Everything in my lectures, I see it at home: cash flow, suppliers, a customer who complains. My parents don't have a degree, and they check every pound. I feel a duty to learn it properly and bring something back to the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one is called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, a useful tool that some people overrate. I use it sometimes for essay outlines, but I check everything. I'd say let's carry on and not get carried away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be worried about my parents' shop more than AI. Rent keeps going up, and big chains are opening nearby. If the shop fails, I'd have to help from my own wages, which are small. I also have a loan, and no one in the family to cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the bakery on weekends and give my mum a hand with the shop's accounts on Sundays. I'd keep studying steadily and look for a summer job at a business where I can learn operations. I'd save part of each pay, even if it's only a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a bit tired. I'm used to carrying things, so it feels normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help with the shop's accounts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents keep everything on paper. I'd put it into a simple spreadsheet so they can see where the money goes each month. My mum doesn't trust computers much, so I'd print the figures and sit with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the shop fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad is fifty-two, and he's done this all his life. He'd find it hard to start again. I'd have to pay some of the household bills, and I'd probably leave university for a year, which I don't want to do.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but overrated**, so let's not get carried away.
I'd say small shops need **fair rents**.
think: I worry about my **parents' shop** more than AI, with rent rising and chains opening.
If it failed, I'd pay household bills from **small wages**.
do: Keep the **bakery weekends** and help my mum with the accounts.
Look for a summer job learning **operations** and save a little.
feel: **Steady** and a bit tired, used to carrying things.
S0.quote: My dad is fifty-two, and he's done this all his life. He'd find it hard to start again.
fieldNote: Kira's mood comes from her **parents' shop**, not her own job.
Uses AI sometimes but checks it, which fits her steady approach.
Willing to pause university if the household needs her.

steps.text: Keep the weekend shifts at the bakery
Put the shop's paper accounts into a simple spreadsheet
Save a little from each pay packet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one is called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, but people have adapted before. Shops and families will need to learn how to use it, without losing what makes them trusted. I'd say that small businesses need support to keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about two things: my degree and my parents' shop. Business graduates do planning, writing and checking, and those are on the card. But a dry-cleaner is hands-on, so it's safer for now. I'd worry that AI could help bigger chains undercut my parents on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI more for study and for the shop: writing a simple website, answering customer messages, and checking prices. I'd teach my parents one thing at a time. I'd also look for an internship at a local firm where I can see how they use these tools, and ask my tutors which skills still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous, but there's something I can do, which makes it better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you get your parents to accept new technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them something that saves them money first, like a message that answers opening hours for them. Dad listens to numbers. If I say it saves two hours a week, he'll try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stays most important to you in all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Trust. People bring their wedding dress to my parents because they know them. A machine can answer messages, but it can't remember someone's name and their mother's dress. I'd protect that.

say: I'd say people have adapted before, but small businesses need **support to keep up**.
I'd say shops must keep what makes them **trusted**.
think: Business graduates do **planning and checking**, which AI takes first.
A dry-cleaner is **hands-on**, but chains could undercut my parents.
do: Use AI to build a simple **website** and answer customer messages for the shop.
Teach my parents **one thing** at a time and find a local internship.
feel: A bit **nervous**, but something I can do makes it better.
S1.quote: People bring their wedding dress to my parents because they know them.
fieldNote: Kira sees **trust** as her family's edge.
Plans to bring technology to her parents gently, using numbers.
Thinks of her degree and the shop together.

steps.text: Build a simple website for my parents' shop with AI help
Show my dad one AI tool that saves two hours a week
Ask a local firm about an internship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one is called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and nobody asked families if they were ready. People should have time to protect what they've built. I'd say it to my parents and to anyone who'll listen at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared. If AI does thinking work by 2028, my degree is gone before I finish, and my parents' savings are all in the shop. Hands-on jobs last longer, so the dry-cleaning shop might survive until the robots come in 2031, but I'm not sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents that night, and ask my tutor if I can switch to something practical. I'd work extra weekends at the bakery and save everything. I'd also help my parents cut costs in the shop and ask the family, aunts and uncles, if they'd help us if things get worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened but determined. I'd feel like I have to hold the family together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what would you do about your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably switch to something that leads to a real job quickly, like accounting for small firms. If I can't, I'd leave and work full time at the shop and the bakery. I don't want to, but family comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say we'll manage, because that's what she always says. My dad would go quiet. They'd both tell me to stay in school, and I'd have to be strong enough to say I might not.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and no one asked families if they were ready.
I'd say people need time to **protect what they've built**.
think: My degree could be gone before I finish, and my parents' **savings** are in the shop.
The shop might last until **2031**, but I'm not sure.
do: Talk to my **parents** that night and ask my tutor about switching course.
Work **extra weekends**, save everything and ask the family for help.
feel: **Frightened but determined**, feeling I must hold the family together.
S2.quote: I'd have to be strong enough to say I might not.
fieldNote: Kira's response is **duty**: she'd hold the family together.
Considers leaving university as a sacrifice.
Expects her mum to say 'we'll manage' and her dad to go quiet.

steps.text: Ask my tutor about switching to small-firm accounting
Work extra weekend shifts at the bakery
Save every spare pound for the shop
Ask my aunts and uncles to help the family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one is called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and everyone should use it. I'd say that families should talk about money now, not later. I'd also say we should look after the older ones, because they'll find it hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I might be okay. I'd finish my degree in 2029 and have two years before the robots arrive in 2034 for hands-on work. I'd want to help my parents change the shop slowly, so they're not caught out. I'd feel a heavy sense of duty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and work for a local firm for a couple of years to learn. I'd help my parents add a delivery service and online booking for the shop. I'd save a thousand a year, and pay off some of my loan early. I'd keep going to church for support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but practical. I like having something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the shop's paperwork in order, so we know what we have. I'd start a savings account in my parents' names that doesn't touch my loan. And I'd learn the basics of the tools so I can teach them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would five years differ from two for your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two they would panic. With five my parents could plan, maybe sell the shop at a good price or hand it to me with proper systems. It makes a difference between losing it and passing it on.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning** and everyone should use it.
I'd say we should **look after older people** who'll find it hard.
think: I'd have two years between my degree and the **robots in 2034**.
I'd feel a heavy sense of **duty** to my parents.
do: Finish the degree, work for a **local firm** and help the shop add delivery.
Save **a thousand a year** and pay off some loan early.
feel: **Anxious but practical**, liking having something to do.
S3.quote: With five my parents could plan, maybe sell the shop at a good price or hand it to me with proper systems.
fieldNote: Kira treats the warning as time to **protect the family business**.
Thinks about handing the shop on, not just surviving.
Her duty is a source of strength and strain.

steps.text: Sort out the shop's paperwork and see what we have
Add online booking and delivery for the shop
Save a thousand a year alongside the loan
Learn the basics of AI tools to teach my parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one is called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and it's best to keep working steadily. I'd say the shop and the family will still be here, and that technology is a tool for people. I'd tell friends to focus on the people around them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel okay. By 2036 I'd be twenty-eight, with a degree, some experience and maybe a business of my own. I'd worry a little that my parents will be too old to adapt, and that I'd be left to carry their worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a company for a few years, and then take over or expand the shop. I'd learn new tools bit by bit, when they're proven. I'd save for a deposit on a small flat for me and my parents, so we're together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. There's room to make a plan and a lot of life in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there's a lot of time, so don't worry yet. I'd ask them to think about what they want for the shop, and I'd say whatever they decide, I'll help. Dad would nod and say nothing, which means he's relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' health, or the shop's rent going up faster than we can pay. That matters more than AI. I'd also worry about being the only one who understands how things work, because then it all falls on me.

say: I'd say ten years is long, so **keep working steadily**.
I'd tell friends to focus on the **people around them**.
think: By 2036 I'd be twenty-eight, with a degree and maybe a **business of my own**.
I'd worry my parents will be too **old to adapt**.
do: Finish the degree, work for a company, then **take over or expand** the shop.
Learn new tools **when proven** and save for a flat for us all.
S4.quote: I'd also worry about being the only one who understands how things work, because then it all falls on me.
fieldNote: Kira's **calm** is real but tied to caring for her parents.
Plans to learn new tools only once they are proven.
Her biggest risk is carrying the family alone.

steps.text: Finish the degree and work for a company first
Save for a deposit on a flat for us all
Ask my parents what they want for the shop
Learn new tools bit by bit when proven

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It lands before my parents can sell or change the shop, and I'd have to hold the family together while giving up my degree. What would help is support for small businesses, fair rents, and honest advice on what to study.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people forget that students from small family businesses carry the shop's worries too. I'm learning management and looking at my parents' accounts at the same time. I just want to make their work count.

headlineQuote: I'm learning management and looking at my parents' accounts at the same time.
portrait: Kira, 18, studies **business management**, lives with her parents who run a dry-cleaning shop, and works weekends at a bakery.
She uses AI sometimes but checks it, and wants to bring technology to her parents **step by step**.
She is traditional and free-market in outlook, valuing trust, family and small business.
Her anxiety is about the **shop's rent and chains**, and her duty to her parents shapes every plan.
The two-year warning alarms her, while ten years lets her plan to take over or expand the shop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because it lands before her parents can change or sell the shop.
whatWouldHelp: Support and **fair rents** for small businesses, and honest advice on what to study.
